messages.author: c0eeebc5f5a22d1e
messages.subject: Specifying positive-only initial parameters
parts:
Hi Stan Team

I have a quick question. I am trying to specify positive-only initial parameters using the "init_r". This is because my nonlinear model has parameters inside a logarithm. 

I have a feeling that this might be why my model occasionally converges beautifully, but then I run the same model again and it falls apart. I can specify init_r=x, which gives random initial parameters between [-x, x]. I tried following the documentation regarding how to specify an input range with lower=0.1, upper=x, but unfortunately wasn't successful. 

My current call to Stan looks like this:
fake.fit <- stan(file="test_model.stan", data=fake.data, iter=500, chains=3, init_r=??)

I've also tried initialising all parameters individually, but it quickly becomes rather messy. Do you have any suggestions?

Thanks for your help!
Chris

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying positive-only initial parameters
parts:
Stan initializes to [-R, R] on the _unconstrained scale.  So if you specify
real<lower=0> x; then it will be log(x) that is randomly initialized to [-R, R],
or x gets initialized to [exp(-R), exp(R)].
On Jan 27, 2017, at 10:04 AM, Chris <chrisva...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Stan Team

I have a quick question. I am trying to specify positive-only initial parameters using the "init_r". This is because my nonlinear model has parameters inside a logarithm. 

I have a feeling that this might be why my model occasionally converges beautifully, but then I run the same model again and it falls apart. I can specify init_r=x, which gives random initial parameters between [-x, x]. I tried following the documentation regarding how to specify an input range with lower=0.1, upper=x, but unfortunately wasn't successful. 

My current call to Stan looks like this:
fake.fit <- stan(file="test_model.stan", data=fake.data, iter=500, chains=3, init_r=??)

I've also tried initialising all parameters individually, but it quickly becomes rather messy. Do you have any suggestions?

Thanks for your help!
Chris

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying positive-only initial parameters
parts:
The initialization routine initializes the parameters only. The
transformed parameters are then constructed from those initial
parameter values deterministically. You are responsible for
ensuring that the transformed parameters have valid values
(certainly there is no way that we could automate that given
the Turing completion of the language). In this case there is
no guarantee that
u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)'

will be positive, hence the failure. This is an ill-posed model.

One suggestion would be to take

beta = exp(u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)’);

but without knowing what your model is trying to do I cannot
offer a better answer.

parts:
Thank you very much for the responses Michael. This group is invaluable. 

My experiments with taking exponentials have been rather unsuccessful so far, with the model losing stability from very large numbers. 

As you can see below, the model is horribly nonlinear. Unfortunately the form of the model is difficult to compromise on, as each parameter has physical significance. a1, a2 and t are predictors, X maps the observations to groups, and the beta are the (all positive) parameters. This is using fake data, with the tight priors on the gamma representing the true values. My question is whether it's possible to extract beta[5] and beta[6] from the data (I've had comparatively less trouble extracting beta[1:4], if I assume fixed values for [5] and [6]). I expect quite strong correlations among some of the parameters. 

The fake data is pretty clean, and nlmer was able to find the true parameters without too much of a nudge.
You'll note this is reasonably similar to the example on pg147 of the reference manual.

data {
  int<lower=1> N;               // number of observations
  int<lower=1> K;               // number of individual predictors
  int<lower=1> J;               // number of groups
  int<lower=1> L;               // number of group predictors (just = 1 currently)
  int<lower=1,upper=J> X[N];    // map group number to observations
  vector[N] y;                  // outcome (logarithm of data)
  matrix[J,L] u;                // group predictors
  real t[N];                    // independent variable
  real a1[N];
  real a2[N];

}
parameters {
  matrix[K, J] z;                             
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[K] tau_unif;

matrix<lower=0>[L, K] gamma;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix<lower=0>[J, K] beta;
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;
  for (k in 1:K) tau[k] = 2.5 * tan(tau_unif[k]);
  beta = u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
}

model {
  to_vector(z) ~ normal(0, 1);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);
  gamma[L,1] ~ normal(0.4, 0.2);
  gamma[L,2] ~ normal(2, 1.5);
  gamma[L,3] ~ normal(2, 0.5);
  gamma[L,4] ~ normal(2, 0.5);
  gamma[L,5] ~ normal(1.5, 0.5);
  gamma[L,6] ~ normal(1.5, 0.5);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(a1[n] - a2[n] 
                  + 1/beta[X[n],6]*log(1+(t[n]/beta[X[n],2])^(beta[X[n],4]*beta[X[n],6])) 
                  - 1/beta[X[n],5]*log(1+(t[n]/beta[X[n],1])^(beta[X[n],3]*beta[X[n],5])),sigma);
}

Much appreciated, genuinely!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying positive-only initial parameters
parts:
Like Michael said, the model may be physically motivated,
but it's ill defined.

Stan requires every value of the parameters satisfying
the constraints to have support in the sense of having
a finite log density. Your definition of beta doesn't
satisfy this property.

The solution is to think through a better model definition,
not to try to initialize near the solution and hope things
don't blow up.

Usually when a model requires a value to be positive,
it uses the log link function to work in the log domain
and then transform the the linear domain through exp().
That will guarantee the values are positive. But it
changes the error scale from normal (additive noise)
to lognormal (multiplicative noise), so you may need
to adjust other bits of the model to match.

- Bob

On Friday, 27 January 2017 11:59:17 UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Like Michael said, the model may be physically motivated,
but it's ill defined.  

Stan requires every value of the parameters satisfying
the constraints to have support in the sense of having
a finite log density.  Your definition of beta doesn't
satisfy this property.

The solution is to think through a better model definition,
not to try to initialize near the solution and hope things
don't blow up.

Usually when a model requires a value to be positive,
it uses the log link function to work in the log domain
and then transform the the linear domain through exp().
That will guarantee the values are positive.  But it
changes the error scale from normal (additive noise)
to lognormal (multiplicative noise), so you may need
to adjust other bits of the model to match.

- Bob

> The initialization routine initializes the parameters only.  The
> transformed parameters are then constructed from those initial
> parameter values deterministically.  You are responsible for
> ensuring that the transformed parameters have valid values
> (certainly there is no way that we could automate that given
> the Turing completion of the language).  In this case there is
> no guarantee that
>
> u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)'
>
> will be positive, hence the failure.  This is an ill-posed model.
>
> One suggestion would be to take
>
> beta = exp(u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)’);
>
> but without knowing what your model is trying to do I cannot
> offer a better answer.
